title: The body as temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, your evening routine: bell, breath, arti, one line. Your line was the day put down. Did you close the day, or did it just stop? Day one hundred and twenty-five.
screen: `YOUR EVENING ROUTINE — THE DAY PUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: For two weeks you've been building a shrine. A corner, a shelf, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a cup of water. You've learned to keep it clean, to bring fresh flowers, to light it at the edges of the day. Now look down. At your hands. Your feet. The chest going up and down. There's a shrine you've been carrying around this whole time, one you didn't have to buy, and most of us treat it worse than the shelf. We skip its meals, cut its sleep, and only notice it when it hurts. A new week starts today, about the body and food. Today: the body as temple.
screen: `TWO WEEKS BUILDING A SHRINE.` → `NOW LOOK DOWN.` → `TODAY: THE BODY AS TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: There's a short line in one of the later Upanishads, the Maitreya Upanishad, that says it straight out: the body is called a temple, and the living one inside it is Shiva himself. The body is the building. What lives in it is holy. You met that idea on day ten, atman: someone is in there. Today's day asks what that means for the building. A twelfth-century poet-saint from Karnataka, Basavanna, said it in a poem people still sing. The rich, he says, build temples for Shiva. What can a poor man do? Then he answers: my legs are the pillars, my body is the shrine, my head is the golden dome. He didn't need stone. He was already standing in one. Here's why this matters on an ordinary Tuesday. If the body is a temple, then looking after it isn't vanity, and it isn't a chore separate from the spiritual life. Bathing before puja, eating with some care, sleeping enough, moving, resting: these become part of the practice, the way sweeping the shrine is part of puja. And notice what the idea doesn't say. It doesn't say the temple has to be perfect, young or strong. A temple can be old. It can be cracked, patched, or hard to climb the steps of. Bodies that are sick, tired, disabled or aging are still temples, and still lived in. The point isn't how it looks. The point is who lives there. This week is about caring for the building.
screen: `THE BODY IS CALLED A TEMPLE.` · `BASAVANNA: MY LEGS ARE THE PILLARS.` · `CARE IS PART OF THE PRACTICE.` · `A TEMPLE CAN BE OLD, OR CRACKED.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever's kinder today. Close your eyes if you like. Start at your feet, the foundation. Just notice them. Move up: the legs, Basavanna's pillars. The belly, moving with the breath. The chest. The hands, which did so much work today. The shoulders, where the day usually hides. The face. The top of the head, the dome. Don't fix anything. Just visit each part, the way you'd walk slowly through a temple. This is where you live. The bell holds the time.
The body as temple. The old idea that the body is a shrine and someone holy lives in it, so caring for it is part of the practice. Today's word.
Your line: this is where you live. Today, do one small kind thing for the building: a glass of water, a stretch, going to bed a little earlier. Day one hundred and twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe before morning puja and treat bodily care, food, rest and movement as part of religious life, drawing on the idea, found in later Upanishads and in devotional poetry, that the body is a temple in which the divine dwells.

fork.setup: you're Basavanna, a poor man in a town where the rich are building grand stone temples for Shiva. what do you do?
options: save for years to build a small one.
say your own body is already the temple.
stop worshipping until you can afford it.
fork.reveal: in his poem, his legs are the pillars, his body the shrine, his head the golden dome. he didn't need stone.

original.note: Sanskrit devālaya: temple, literally a house of God. The Maitreya Upanishad calls the body one.

trapdoor: what you thought: take care of yourself, spiritually speaking.
what it means: the body is a shrine, and someone holy lives in it, so caring for it is part of worship, whatever state it's in.

what a scholar hears: Maitreya Upanishad 2.1 reads deho devalayah proktah, sa jivah kevalah shivah; Basavanna's vachana, part of the twelfth-century Virashaiva movement, sets the moving body against the standing temple.

sources.ref: Maitreya (Maitreyi) Upanishad 2.1 (the body is called a temple; the living being is Shiva)

notes: Please confirm the Maitreya Upanishad 2.1 reference and text (deho devalayah proktah...); some editions call it Maitreyi Upanishad.
Basavanna's vachana is paraphrased; the well-known English version (A.K. Ramanujan, 1973) is under copyright and is not quoted.

Basavanna's poem is often read as a critique of temple-building by the wealthy; the script presents it gently, as a poor man's answer. Confirm the tone is fair to temple worship, which week 20 teaches.
The inclusive line about sick, disabled and aging bodies is an application, not a textual claim.
